messages.subject: Counting from one habitat; include animals detected in another habitat?
messages.subject_clean: Counting from one habitat; include animals detected in another habitat?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone,

I have a slightly complicated situation, and I would appreciate people’s thoughts on the appropriate way to proceed. Apologies for the long background description.

I have multi-species bird point count data collected in a range of habitat types, including continuous forest and open farmland. Unsurprisingly, detectability varies between habitat type. (I checked this by comparing pooled CDS and MCDS with habitat as a covariate, and AIC always selects the MCDS models).

In some cases the habitat patches were so large that I could be certain that the intervening habitat was uniform. However, in others (particularly the farmland) there are lots of small patches of different habitat (e.g. fields, forest fragments etc.) So just because I was counting in a field, doesn’t mean that I couldn’t detect a bird singing in a forest patch 200m away. And in that situation, I could detect that species at a much greater distance than I could have if it had just been uniform forest between me and the bird.

Point count locations were assigned randomly, so birds’ distributions should not be influenced by them directly. However, birds were distributed non-randomly with respect to habitat, as species are often habitat-specific (i.e. the forest-adapted birds are only going to be in the forest patches and not in the fields). I can’t lump the detections of those forest birds in farmland together with detections of the same species from the continuous forest because the calls will have attenuated in different ways between the habitats. However, I sense that it would also be wrong ignore the habitat differences, and treat all of the farmland detections as if they came from a uniform habitat.

Therefore, would it be better to only include those species that I detected in the same habitat in which I was counting? (i.e. only include birds detected in fields when I was standing in fields, and discarding those detected in forest patches). Alternatively, I may be over-thinking this. The dataset is fairly large (~10,000 detections per habitat), and there are many point counts, in multiple landscapes with different configurations. So perhaps the effect of the patchy landscape will even out across the whole dataset.

In addition, should I run stratified analyses for each habitat type, or am I able to stick with the MCDS model with habitat as a covariate, and just produce abundance estimates in that way?

I would be interested to hear others’ opinions about my reasoning and intended approach.

Thanks in advance,

Tom

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Counting from one habitat; include animals detected in another habitat?
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Counting from one habitat; include animals detected in another habitat?
messages.body_plain:
Tom, yes, I think you are over-thinking it.  If your aim is just to estimate abundance (or density), then you can just analyse data from all points together.  You can use MCDS and use for example an open-ness covariate, but even if you ignore the big differences in detectability between points and use CDS, pooling robustness means that you get very little bias in your estimates.  (You can try it both ways to verify this.)  By pooling the data, you will need to choose a truncation distance that’s satisfactory in woodland, so you will end up truncating a lot of your detections in open habitat.

Pooling robustness doesn’t apply if you need to estimate density separately by habitat type, so mcds is better for that.  As you note, classifying habitat type is problematic, because of its patchy nature.  You can stratify your area by habitat type, and for points in one habitat from which you detect birds in a second habitat, you can include those detections when analysing densities in that second habitat.  The discussion in the 2004 adv ds book on buffer zones is relevant here.  But it gets a bit messy.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
There is no single right way to do this.  What you can do is define habitat strata, and divide your survey region into strata.  It is up to you whether you combine small patches of woodland with continuous forest.  My comment was simply to indicate that you can include detections made in a given habitat from a point in another habitat in your analysis for the first habitat.  This issue is discussed on pp192-194 of the 2004 adv ds book.

Steve

messages.subject: Can transects be run over multiple days?
messages.subject_clean: Can transects be run over multiple days?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We are designing a distance sampling study using the line-transect method. Our plan was to have 10 randomly places transects driven 1x/month. However, once we field tested the methods, we realized that all 10 transects will not be able to be run in a single day due to rocky roads, distance between transect, etc.

We are trying to figure out some solutions...would we be able to drive the 10 transects over a period of a couple days? 5 randomly picked transects would be driven the first day and the remaining 5 transects would be driven the second day. We are hesitate to do this based on the assumption of Distance that all animals do not move. Are there any issues with running the a system of transects over multiple days instead of over just one day?

Thanks so much for your help and feedback,
Jenna

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Can transects be run over multiple days?
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Can transects be run over multiple days?
messages.body_plain:
Jenna, absolutely no problem with that.  Provided there isn’t likely to be a systematic movement of animals between the two days, there is no issue with movement.  (If movement is random, then on average, for each animal moving from the region you cover on day 1 to the region you cover on day 2, there will be one going the other way, so on average, movement does not generate bias.)  Bias arising from animal movement can arise either because animals respond to the observer or because observer speed is not appreciably greater than animal speed.  Neither of those have anything to do with animals moving from one transect to another;  the animal speed issue is because, if you travel slowly and animals move fast, you’ll get many animals moving onto your strip while in detection range that were not there initially.  The faster the observer moves relative to average animal speed, the smaller the bias.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm working on distance sampling with R to estimate abundance and density of a bird population. My study uses the point transect method.
Data contain observation point data of 10 years in 2 different regions (Region.Label)

My data used for DS contain the following columns
"Region.Label" (South or East), "Sample.Label" (ID of the observation point), "Effort", "distance", "Area", "size", "year", "Point", "Xcoord", "Ycoord" (coordinates of latitude and longitude).

I tests different model for the Detection function.
For the first 2 models, it works well:
mod1 <- ds(DSdata, truncation = list(left=0, right=3.1), transect = "point", formula=~Region.Label, key = "hn")
mod2 <- ds(DSdata, truncation = list(left=0, right=3.1), transect = "point", formula=~Region.Label+year, key = "hn")

I would like to know how can i integrate covariate's interaction in my model.
Usually, in R, for some different model (not in distance sampling) I write it like that:  Region.Label*Year, or Region.Label+Year+ Region.Label*Year or Region.Label:Year.

But when I try this:
mod3 <- ds(DSdata, truncation = list(left=0, right=3.1), transect = "point", formula=~Region.Label*year, key = "hn")
No models could be fitted.

It is a writing problem of "formula=" ?
I don't know how to solve this problem.

Thank you for your help and feedback,

sorry for my english i hope you'll understand the sense of my SOS.

Alice

I don't know about the quantity of data you have, but I suspect the message you received is not an error message, but rather because the job of fitting a detection function to your data is actually too difficult.  The notation you have provided is correct, so that is not the problem.

The model you have requested (with strata and year as interacting covariates) is asking that a 20 parameter detection function be fitted.  I suspect there are one or more of the stratum/year combinations you have few data and this is causing model fitting challenges for the software.

Given your data are in R, you can do a quick tablulation of how many data you have to fit a model with as many parameters as these.  You note that you can fit a model with simply stratum (10 parameters) or stratum+year (11 parameters) the software succeeds in producing detection function parameter estimates, but with the most complex model, the challenge is too great.

I hope this answers your question.

Thanks in advance for sharing your experiences with me.

Marco

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling and urban environment
messages.body_plain:
Marco

There are considerable challenges when trying to use line transect sampling in an urban environment.  Detectability is not strictly a function of distance as some birds will be on rooftops and invisible even at close distances.

Also, the transects cannot be randomly placed.  You will be forced to travel along streets, and you cannot travel through buildings; leading to non-random sampling.

Yet another challenge:  Distance sampling assumes that density of animals is the same at all distances from the transect; stated another way, animals are distributed independently of the transect.  This is the so-called "design assumption" Buckland et al. (2015) Section 1.7

If you examine the one paper on distance sampling of urban pigeons (Giunchi et al. 2007, http://eprints.adm.unipi.it/521/1/Article_cat.pdf) you will see an absence of detections close to the transect.  The cause of this is not that detectability was difficult, but rather because pigeons were unlikely to rest in the middle of the streets used as transects by these investigators.

They employed left-truncation which is a remedy that does not directly address the issue of non-uniform distribution with respect to the transect.

It is difficult to adequately sample habitats in an urban environment, whether it be for pigeons or feral dogs and cats.

messages.subject: significant detection covariates in a dsm
messages.subject_clean: significant detection covariates in a dsm
messages.body_plain:
Hello again, I've had a somewhat interesting development in my density surface modelling for arctic songbirds. While trying to deal with the problem of overdispersion by adding potentially missing covariates to the model, I included a couple of the covariates actually used in the fitting of my candidate set of detection functions. In particular, start time of survey popped out as being highly significant in my dsm. Start time was not a significant covariate in my detection function modelling. In my survey design I sampled at all hours of the day (although mostly between mid morning and afternoon) assuming that due to the near 24 hour daylight for most of the summer and published research on the subject, that the typical daily activity patterns for songbirds (and other avian species) would be relaxed in the arctic (also because of the necessity of fitting sampling protocol in between other aspects of our research program).

It seems to me this is a pretty important catch. That start time of survey was not important in the fitting of the detection function but was important in the dsm to me indicates that it probably caused birds to not be detected at all in some of my surveys. Non-counts obviously cannot be adjusted with a detection function, and so not taking this into account (or not designing your sampling protocol properly), could lead to zero inflation of your dataset and cause you to very much underestimate true abundance. Is my reading of this situation plausible? Is including detection covariates in a density surface model fair game?

As a side note, i also fit a zero inflated mixture model to my data, including start time in both the main and zero inflated portion of the model - start time was only significant in the zero inflated portion of the model, which seems to fit with my intuition so far.

Interested to hear someone's take on this who has more knowledge/experience than me.

Kevin

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] significant detection covariates in a dsm
messages.body_plain:
Kevin, that is likely the case.  For species that are mostly detected by song, if some individuals stop singing for periods during the day, they are likely to be undetected during such periods.  In theory, if you’re still certain to detect them on the line or at the point, all should be OK, but if quiet birds move away from the observer, they may well escape detection.  Similarly, females are often undetected.  For temperate songbird surveys, it is often a good strategy to carry out surveys at peak singing season, at times of day when song is greatest, and to record only singing males, with a view to estimating the number of territories.

Steve Buckland

I'm interested in guanacos density in every period.  I was reading that one alternative is to pool all data from the 2 repeated visits in each period into a single line transect prior to analysis and to record the effort as transect length multiplied by 2 visits (in my case effort=20km). And for every period I should run a separate model.

-Is that alternative OK even though the visits are not close in time? Do I have to put this in an argument in the ds function?

-Should I do the same when I prepare the segments for dsm? So, in the same segment, I will have counts of the animals from, for example, September 2014 and 2016?

Thank you very much in advance!

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] repeated transects in diffrent years
messages.body_plain:
Antonella

I take it you wish to produce estimates for 6 time periods Sept14, Dec14, Feb15(?), Sept16, Dec16, Feb17(?).   During each of those time periods, you conducted 2 surveys.  I hope that is correct and is the basis for my answer, although your email subject makes me wonder whether you conducted 1 or 2 surveys each year. Combining the data (number of detections and cumulative effort) across the 2 surveys would be the proper way to produce a density estimate for each of the 6 periods.  There is nothing special you need to add as an argument to ds() if you double the effort (transect length) in your data as you describe.

If however, you are combining data across years, that might be less advisable.  If you have sufficient detections in each year, it might be better to produce separate analyses for each year.

For the DSM analysis, the data would be combined in the identical way the data were combined for the detection function modelling.

If I have misunderstood your design or your question, please correct me.

messages.subject: Importing date fields into Distance 7.1
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

When using the import wizard in Distance 7.1 for Windows, is it possible to import date (DD/MM/YYYY) fields and set them to a proper 'date' format rather than 'integer', 'decimal' or 'text'? Or, is the only solution to change them to something like Julian date and format them as 'decimal'?

Thanks
Esther

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Importing date fields into Distance 7.1
messages.body_plain:
Hi Esther, (cc list)

Yup, I'm afraid that Distance is only designed to cope with integer,
decimal or text.  Your Julian date solution seems a good one, except I
think it would be better as an integer than a decimal.  If you have
multi-year data, and want to preserve that info, then you could set the
date of the first survey as day 0 and count forward from there (or use
some other start day - when I were a nipper, computers used to use Jan
1st 1970 as day zero... oh, those were the days...).

Best wishes, Len

messages.subject: Re: repeated transects in diffrent years
messages.body_plain:
Antonella

I'm under the impression you traveled the same transects in 2014 and 2016.  That suggests to me your data will not be more spatially representative by pooling the data.

If you intend to use time-varying covariates in your density surface modelling, you would not pool data across years.

There is no magic number regarding number of segments.  Asked another way, what should a segment size be.  A broad rule of thumb is for segment length to be roughly twice the distance sampling truncation distance.  But segment size should have some relationship to the granularity of the covariates used in the density surface model.  A uniform environment might have large segments, a heterogeneous environment will have small segments.

Sorry there are not "clean" rules on this subject.
